title: Coaxing, Cajoling and Threatening Subscribers: the Baring Guarantee, Argentina's Default, and the Inquiry Parliament Refused
participants: The two major banks of Buenos Aires
Mr Goschen, Chancellor of the Exchequer

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Not quantified by any source read for this dossier, and nothing is invented. What is recorded is the structure of the rescue: a guarantee fund "which would be called on if the Bank-supervised liquidation of Baring's assets was not sufficient" — a backstop behind a liquidation, not a payment to the house.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The standing structural complaint reached the Commons within a fortnight, in a Member's words: "the continual annual strain put upon business by the decrease in the Bank reserve, and constant scarcity of gold", under an Act of 1844 that was no longer "in keeping with the present time, and the expansion of business which has taken place since the Act was passed". On the other side of the same paper sat a sovereign whose crisis was, in the NBER paper's words, "a triple crisis involving a banking meltdown, a currency crisis and a suspension of payments on national debt".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is in the naming, and it runs through Parliament. The only parliamentary reference found to the episode calls it "the recent serious crisis in the City"; neither "Baring" nor "Argentine" appears anywhere in the debate. A rescue large enough to require the Governor of the Bank of England to assemble a subscription list reached the floor of the Commons once, as an adjective.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The rescue, as the NBER paper read on a parallel branch records it: "Bank of England governor William Lidderdale set about assembling subscribers to a guarantee fund" and "placed the Bank of England's name at the top of the list for £1 million and set about coaxing, cajoling, and, in some cases, even threatening potential subscribers." The house was carried by a fund the Bank organised and headed. The sovereign was not: "The government of Argentina suspended payments on its debts. The two major banks of Buenos Aires were liquidated in 1890."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: This stage the Hansard record delivers cleanly. Asked whether the Government would appoint a Royal Commission "to inquire into the whole question of the working of the Bank Act of 1844", Mr Goschen answered: "No, Sir; we have no such intention. If at any time it should appear to Her Majesty's Government that the arrangements made in 1844 should be altered in any particulars, they would prefer to deal with the matter on their own initiative and responsibility rather than to relegate the matter to a Royal Commission." Asked about amending the Act, he was "not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act". Within days of Parliament reconvening after the guarantee, an inquiry was refused and a policy statement declined.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Bank Charter Act 1844 and the reserve arrangements it fixed — the statute whose suspension by Treasury letter the Commons had debated in 1847, 1857 and 1866 — and a London house underwriting a sovereign's debt with no mechanism for its own failure.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A subscribed guarantee fund led by the central bank's own name, standing behind a Bank-supervised liquidation — a rescue by organised private subscription rather than by Treasury letter. And nothing in statute: the Government declined both an amending Bill and a Royal Commission.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The underwriter is carried by a fund its own regulator organises; the sovereign whose debt caused it defaults and loses its banks; the legislature asks whether the governing statute should be examined; the executive says it would rather decide alone; and the arrangement survives unexamined into the next crisis.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Bank of England bailed out Barings with public money in November 1890, and buried it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The money was subscribed, not appropriated, and it was a guarantee, not a grant: a fund "which would be called on if the Bank-supervised liquidation of Baring's assets was not sufficient", headed by the Bank of England's own £1 million and filled by subscribers the Governor spent his time "coaxing, cajoling, and, in some cases, even threatening". Whether any of it was ever called is not in what was read. The burial half is closer to the record than the bailout half, and Hansard is the evidence: across the November and December 1890 and January and February 1891 sittings, searched by debate title for "Baring", "Argentine", "Bank of England", "Bank Act", "gold reserve", "money market" and "financial", the episode reaches the floor once, unnamed, and the one request for an inquiry into the statute that had just been tested is answered "No, Sir; we have no such intention." What makes this a ledger entry is not where the money came from but who was and was not reached by it. The house that had underwritten the paper was carried. The sovereign on the other side of it suspended payments and lost both its major banks the same year. ON SOURCING: this dossier was built in two halves by two sessions. The Hansard exchange was read here; the two NBER working papers were fetched and verified through glm-recheck --strict-sources on a parallel branch and are carried in at the merge with that stated in each citation. Both are academic secondary sources, and the parallel session recorded that its own check corrected it twice — it had drafted "loans from the Banque de France and Russia", which the sources do not carry, and a list of seven Latin American defaults, which they do not carry either. Neither is asserted here. No Bank of England record of November 1890 was read by either session, and the terms of the guarantee, the names of the subscribers and the fate of the fund are not asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A single exchange in the House of Commons on 27 November 1890, Hansard vol 349 c125: Mr Ernest Spencer's question whether, "in view of the recent serious crisis in the City", the Government would consider a short Bill to amend the Bank Act of 1844 by issuing £1 notes; Mr Goschen's reply that he was "not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act"; Mr Lea's question whether a Royal Commission would be appointed to inquire into the working of the Act; and Mr Goschen's reply, "No, Sir; we have no such intention", with a stated preference for acting "on their own initiative and responsibility". This is the only debate heading on the crisis found across the sittings of November and December 1890 and January and February 1891, and it does not name the firm. NBER Working Paper 20832, as verified on a parallel branch: that Governor William Lidderdale "set about assembling subscribers to a guarantee fund which would be called on if the Bank-supervised liquidation of Baring's assets was not sufficient" and "placed the Bank of England's name at the top of the list for £1 million and set about coaxing, cajoling, and, in some cases, even threatening potential subscribers." NBER Working Paper 11173, as verified on the same branch: that in Argentina "this crisis was a triple crisis involving a banking meltdown, a currency crisis and a suspension of payments on national debt", that "The government of Argentina suspended payments on its debts", and that "The two major banks of Buenos Aires were liquidated in 1890."

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE BANK ACT—£1 NOTES.", HC Deb 27 November 1890 vol 349 c125 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service; the entire exchange is quoted below, because it is short and because its brevity is the point. MR. ERNEST SPENCER (West Bromwich): "I beg to ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether, in view of the recent serious crisis in the City, and the continual annual strain put upon business by the decrease in the Bank reserve, and constant scarcity of gold, the Government will now consider the advisability of introducing a short Bill to amend the Bank Act of 1844 by the issue of £1 notes against silver, or Consols, or otherwise, in order that it may be in keeping with the present time, and the expansion of business which has taken place since the Act was passed?" MR. GOSCHEN: "I am not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act, nor am I prepared to admit the second part of my hon. Friend's question as a necessary corollary to the first." MR. LEA (Londonderry, S.): "I have also to ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer if the Government intend to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the whole question of the working of the Bank Act of 1844; if so, when such Royal Commission will be appointed?" MR. GOSCHEN: "No, Sir; we have no such intention. If at any time it should appear to Her Majesty's Government that the arrangements made in 1844 should be altered in any particulars, they would prefer to deal with the matter on their own initiative and responsibility rather than to relegate the matter to a Royal Commission." WHAT THIS IS AND WHAT IT IS NOT. It is the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the first week Parliament sat after the November 1890 rescue, refusing an inquiry into the statute governing the Bank of England's reserve, and stating a preference for acting "on their own initiative and responsibility" instead. It is also the only occasion found, across the whole of the November and December 1890 and the January and February 1891 sittings, on which the episode reaches the floor at all: the sitting indexes for those months were searched by title for "Baring", "Argentine", "Bank of England", "Bank Act", "gold reserve", "money market" and "financial", and this is the only debate heading about the crisis. THE FIRM IS NEVER NAMED. Mr Spencer says only "the recent serious crisis in the City"; neither "Baring" nor "Argentine" appears. Nothing here describes the rescue, its terms, who guaranteed what, or who gained or lost by it, and no such claim is made from this source. The Bank of England's own records of November 1890 were not read.
